title: Morality must always come before the law
subtitle: The law is often morally wrong
author: Michael Huemer
introduction: Most people think that the law safeguards morality. Some even argue that since morality is subjective, and our legal system is a record of this, the law cannot be wrong. But in this article, philosopher Michael Huemer argues that the law is often morally wrong, and morality must always come before the law.
body:
In 2007, a man named Anthony Crutcher was arrested in Mississippi for selling a total of about $40 worth of cocaine (in multiple transactions) to a police informant. Per federal sentencing guidelines, in view of his two prior drug convictions, Mr. Crutcher was sentenced to 60 years in prison. It is hard to believe that anyone would deem this a just sentence. It is, indeed, questionable whether any punishment is merited for such a crime: after all, individuals have a right to put whatever they want into their own bodies, and Crutcher was merely helping a competent, informed adult to exercise that right. But whatever you think of that argument, it is difficult to imagine any conception of proportionality on which Crutcher’s crime merited a sentence of 60 years.

Cases like these raise questions about the relationship between morality and the law. Can the law be morally wrong? Why do we have laws in the first place? And what should we do when the law conflicts with our sense of morality?

SUGGESTED VIEWING Morality and prejudice With Tommy J. Curry, Michael Huemer, Melis Erdur, Barry C. Smith

Begin with the first question: Can the law be wrong? Some might argue that morality is a social construct, that the law is how society declares what is right and wrong, and that therefore the law itself cannot be morally wrong. The best way to refute such a view is by examples: Slavery was always wrong, as were the laws enforcing it. If you lived in the American South before the Civil War, you ought not to have owned slaves. If you discovered a runaway slave, it would have been morally wrong to report them, even though this was legally required. If America somehow re-introduces slavery, you should not participate in the practice.

In Nazi Germany, the persecution of Jews was legally enforced. Nevertheless, if you lived in that time, it would have been wrong for you to participate in persecuting Jews. Oscar Schindler – the businessman who famously saved about 1200 Jews from the concentration camps – was a hero, not a villain, for going against the practices of his society and government.

Nearly everyone can see these points. They show that morality does not merely derive from the law. We have the capacity to judge the law itself, and sometimes it comes up wanting.

If there were no objective demands of justice, then there would be no reason to have laws and no reason to punish anyone for violating them. If everyone always obeyed the demands of justice of their own accord, there would again be no need for laws.

This leads us to our second question: Why, in general, should we have laws? The answer is that the law properly serves to enforce a certain part of morality. Morality, in the philosophers’ sense, consists of non-selfish, categorical, objective reasons for action. That is, a person has reasons for behaving in certain ways which are not based on self-interest, not based on one’s own desires, and not based on conventions or observers’ attitudes towards those forms of behavior. These are broadly “moral reasons”. There is also a subset of moral reasons that are concerned with justice, or what individuals have a right to demand of each other. You have a right to demand, for example, that others pay their debts, keep their agreements, refrain from violence, refrain from stealing or damaging each other’s property.

The law exists, or ought to exist, to enforce these demands of justice. If there were no objective demands of justice, then there would be no reason to have laws and no reason to punish anyone for violating them. If everyone always obeyed the demands of justice of their own accord, there would again be no need for laws. We need laws because there are preexisting demands of justice, and some individuals either fail to perceive them or simply choose to violate them; thus, some sort of enforcement is needed. And if we as a society are enforcing certain demands, with punishments coercively imposed for violations, then we are obligated to make it sufficiently clear to all what demands we are enforcing. This is done, in our society, by recording these demands in law books.

Unfortunately, human beings are flawed, and everything we do is subject to error and/or corruption. Sometimes, lawmakers will use their power to enforce irrational prejudices or to wrongly promote their own interests at the expense of others, instead of just enforcing the demands of justice. Thus it happens that some laws are morally wrong.

This leads to our third question: What should one do when the law is substantively wrong? The answer is that morality must come before the law. The law is only a tool for enforcing (a subset of) morality. A means cannot be more important than the end that it serves, and a tool cannot be more important than the purpose for which that tool exists. If, therefore, you know that a law is substantively wrong, then you have no moral reason for obeying or helping to enforce that law.

You may of course still have practical reasons to obey the law; for instance, I highly recommend avoiding illegal drug use when such behavior is likely to be detected by the police. But this is for self-interested reasons, not moral reasons. In some cases, you may even have moral reasons to avoid drug use, such as if you are pregnant or responsible for caring for children. My point is merely that the illegality of drug use does not give you any added moral reason to refrain.

Thus, if you had served on the jury in the case of Anthony Crutcher, knowing that he faced an unjustly disproportionate sentence if convicted, you should have voted “not guilty”, regardless of the factual evidence.

Some people object that it is not possible for individuals to reliably tell when the law is morally wrong, that there will be substantial disagreement about such things, and therefore that we should stick to the easier task of simply enforcing the written law. In response, it is true that we do not always know when the law is wrong; nevertheless, at least sometimes we know – and when we do, we should avoid enforcing such laws. This is no different from any other norm that has exceptions; for example, it is usually wrong to lie, but sometimes it is right, and at least sometimes we can tell this – so there is no need to proclaim, absurdly, that we should never lie.

Suppose you disagree with me; suppose you think that one can never know that a law is immoral. If so, then I think you should, to remain coherent, claim that no one can ever know any moral truth. For the way in which I would know that certain laws are wrong is no different from how I know any other moral truth. If I can’t know that it is wrong to send someone to prison for 60 years for selling $40 worth of cocaine, then why would I be able to know that stealing is wrong, or that murder is wrong, or that breaking the law is wrong?

Government officials are no better positioned than I am; if I don’t know any moral truths, they don’t either. And if they don’t know any moral truths, then they have no reason to make or enforce any laws. There would be no reason for the legislature to outlaw stealing if the legislators don’t know whether stealing is wrong. Nor would there be any reason for courts to punish criminals if they don’t know whether breaking the law is wrong, nor whether punishing criminals is right.

In sum, the reasons that we have for making and enforcing laws in the first place presuppose some knowledge of independently-existing moral truths, which the laws should serve to enforce. When the law conflicts with this end, it should no longer be respected.
